First Law of Thermodynamics
Heat supplied to a system = increase in internal energy + work done by the system. Simply: conservation of energy for thermal systems.
Q = ΔU + W
Money analogy: You receive ₹100 (Q). You save ₹60 (ΔU) and spend ₹40 (W). Q = ΔU + W.

Applications
ProcessConditionFirst Law Becomes
IsothermalΔU = 0Q = W
AdiabaticQ = 0W = −ΔU
IsochoricW = 0Q = ΔU
IsobaricP = constQ = ΔU + PΔV
CyclicΔU = 0Q = W
Solved: Gas absorbs 200 J, does 80 J of work → ΔU = 200 − 80 = 120 J

Thermodynamics

The branch of physics dealing with the conversion of heat into work and vice versa, studying energy transfer between a system and surroundings.

System Types

  • Open System: Both energy and matter can transfer (e.g., boiling water in open pot)
  • Closed System: Only energy transfers, no matter (e.g., gas in sealed cylinder)
  • Isolated System: No energy or matter transfer (e.g., ideal thermos flask)

Thermal Equilibrium
Two systems are in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature — no net heat flow between them even in thermal contact.
Example: Hot tea left in a room eventually reaches room temperature. After that — no more heat flows. They are in thermal equilibrium.

Kelvin-Planck Statement (Heat Engines)
It is impossible to build a device that converts ALL heat from a single reservoir completely into work in a cycle.
Simple: No engine can be 100% efficient. Some heat must always be rejected to a cold sink.

Carnot Refrigerator
Reverse Carnot — uses work to move heat from cold to hot body (like a fridge). COP can be greater than 1.
COP = Q₂/W = T₂ / (T₁ − T₂)

Solved Examples
Ex 1: Source 600 K, Sink 300 K, absorbs 1000 J
η = 1 − 300/600 = 50%  |  W = 500 J  |  Q₂ = 500 J
Ex 2: η = 40%, rejects 600 J to sink
Q₁ = 600/0.6 = 1000 J  |  W = 400 J

Heat (Q)
Energy transferred between system and surroundings due to temperature difference.
Q > 0 → heat absorbed by system  |  Q < 0 → heat released

Example: Heating gas in a sealed rigid container — pressure rises, no expansion.

Specific Heat Capacities — Cᵥ and Cₚ
Cᵥ — heat to raise 1 mol by 1K at constant volume. All heat → internal energy.
Cₚ — heat to raise 1 mol by 1K at constant pressure. Heat → internal energy + expansion work.
Cₚ − Cᵥ = R    (Mayer's Relation, R = 8.314 J/mol·K)
γ = Cₚ / Cᵥ    (always > 1)
Gas TypeCᵥCₚγExamples
Monatomic3R/25R/21.67He, Ne, Ar
Diatomic5R/27R/21.4N₂, O₂, H₂
Triatomic+3R4R1.33CO₂, H₂O

Work (W)
Energy transferred when a system changes its volume against external pressure.
W = PΔV = P(V₂ − V₁)
General: W = ∫PdV = Area under P-V curve
Expansion (V₂ > V₁): W > 0 (work done BY system)
Compression (V₂ < V₁): W < 0 (work done ON system)
⚠ Q and W are path functions — their values depend on the process, not just start & end states.

Clausius Statement (Refrigerators)
Heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body without external work being done.
Simple: A fridge needs electricity to move heat from cold inside to warm room. It doesn't happen on its own.

Carnot Engine — Definition
An ideal, reversible heat engine operating between a hot source (T₁) and cold sink (T₂). Has the maximum possible efficiency for any engine between those two temperatures.
η = 1 − T₂/T₁    (T must be in Kelvin!)
η = W/Q₁ = (Q₁ − Q₂) / Q₁
⚠ η = 100% only if T₂ = 0 K (absolute zero) — physically impossible. So no engine is ever 100% efficient.

Adiabatic — No Heat Exchange
Q = 0  |  PVᵞ = const  |  W = −ΔU
W = nR(T₁ − T₂) / (γ − 1)
Expansion: Gas cools — tyre bursting, aerosol spray feels cold.
Compression: Gas heats — bicycle pump gets warm, diesel ignition.

data.content:
✅ Zeroth Law: A↔C, B↔C ⟹ A↔B — defines temperature
✅ First Law: Q = ΔU + W
✅ Work by gas: W = PΔV = ∫PdV
✅ Ideal gas: PV = nRT
✅ Mayer's relation: Cₚ − Cᵥ = R
✅ Adiabatic index: γ = Cₚ/Cᵥ (1.67 / 1.4 / 1.33)
✅ Isothermal work: W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁)
✅ Adiabatic eq: PVᵞ = const
✅ Adiabatic work: W = nR(T₁−T₂)/(γ−1)
✅ Carnot efficiency: η = 1 − T₂/T₁
✅ Carnot work: W = η × Q₁
✅ COP (refrigerator): COP = T₂/(T₁−T₂)
✅ Isochoric heat: Q = nCᵥΔT
✅ Isobaric heat: Q = nCₚΔT

Common Mistakes
❌ Using °C instead of Kelvin in Carnot formula
❌ Treating Q and W as state functions (they are NOT)
❌ Assuming Carnot can be 100% efficient
❌ Confusing Cᵥ and Cₚ — Cₚ is always larger
❌ Thinking First Law can be violated — it never is

Reversible vs Irreversible Processes
PropertyReversibleIrreversible
SpeedInfinitely slowFinite speed
FrictionZeroPresent
EfficiencyMaximum possibleLess than maximum
ExistenceIdeal / theoreticalAll real processes
ExampleVery slow compressionBurning fuel, mixing
⚡ All natural processes are irreversible. Reversible processes give the upper limit of efficiency.

Internal Energy (U)
Total energy stored inside a system — kinetic energy of molecules (random motion) + potential energy (intermolecular forces).
For ideal gas: U = nCᵥT    (depends only on T)
⚡ U is a state function — depends only on current state (P,V,T), not on the path taken.

Isobaric — Constant Pressure
P = const  |  W = PΔV = nRΔT  |  Q = nCₚΔT
Example: Boiling water at atmospheric pressure — expands into steam at constant P.

Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
If A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are also in thermal equilibrium with each other.
A ↔ C and B ↔ C ⟹ A ↔ B
This law is the basis of temperature measurement. C acts as a thermometer.
Why "Zeroth"? It was formulated after First & Second Laws but is more fundamental — it defines temperature itself.
